articles.title: Turkey: Several pupils injured in shooting outside school
articles.summary: The shooter, a pupil, allegedly took a rifle and shot indiscriminately at his schoolmates in front of their high school. Turkey was shocked by two back-to-back school shootings earlier this year.

image.caption: Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the schoolImage: DHA

blocks.text: A shooting near a high school in Turkey's Manisa province resulted in at least 11 injured pupils, two of whom were in critical condition on Tuesday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.
The shooter, a pupil at the school, was arrested together with both of his parents and his grandfather.
What do we know about the shooting incident?
The suspect is said to have taken the weapon from his grandparents' house, with his grandfather believed to have had a licence for it.
Local authorities said the attack took place at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district at about 08:00am local time (07:00 CET).
The motive for the shooting is also under investigation. Some reports suggest the student had suffered from bullying.

blocks.caption: Two back-to-back school shootings in April left around 10 killed and dozens more injuredImage: Ensar Ozdemir/REUTERS

blocks.text: "When the ​security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any ​negligence, any irresponsibility to be overlooked," the minister posted on his X account.

"The ‌circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon's storage, the parents' obligations regarding care ‌and supervision, and allegations of bullying prior to the incident ‌are ​being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles," Gurlek added.
Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the school, while police told families to stay away from the area.
Gun control tightened after school shootings
School shootings are rare in Turkey, but this year alone saw two back-to-back shootings that shocked the nation.
Two school shootings that took place in April resulted in the tightening of gun controls and the increase of security measures at educational facilities as the academic year started last week.
Several students and their teacher were killed in one of the attacks, with the other resulting in 16 people being injured.
According to Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, 31,000 school supervisors and police officers on duty were assigned to school seen as being at risk, as per a new measure introduced only on Monday.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan responded to the latest shooting attack by promising even tighter gun controls.
"When we look at similar attacks around the world, especially in the United States, we see one of the perpetrators' aims is to terrorise society," the Turkish leader said.

articles.title: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses
articles.summary: 'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips

blocks.text: Graphics by Nico Villarete/Rappler
'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips
Even the country’s top fast food chain was not spared in the expansive investigation into Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
Could Jollibee hold a piece of the smoking gun that the prosecution has been searching for to remove her from office?

Jollibee was implicated in the mess because documents show that its Bolton Street branch in Davao City is owned by Gencorp Industries Inc., described in one of government documents as a franchisee of the casual dining giant.

Duterte said in her sworn Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she is a stockholder of Gencorp, although her name is not in Securities and Exchange Commission documents (SEC) filings of the company.

Other companies associated with the Vice President or her husband Mans Carpio are Metro City Chow Food Corporation, City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation, Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.
The names of several of these companies appear to echo those of Jollibee and its sister fast-food chain, Chowking.

“This P2.1 billion in sales — these are restaurants, right? Are they Jollibee or Chowking?” Senator Kiko Pangilinan asked. “I would assume there are many Jollibee and Chowking franchises, which is why sales reached billions over a period of time.”
“One of the financial statements that the witness identified yesterday contains the word ‘Jollibee’ in reference to Gencorp,” prosecutor Erwin Matib said. “Yes, there are franchises.”
Jollibee Davao Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes. It is in the same building as the listed address of Gencorp.

Rappler previously reported that Gencorp has cornered at least P14 million in contracts with Davao City Hall since 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became VP, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown.

The Davao City mayor later not only confirmed the existence of the deals, but even updated the actual total value of the contracts bagged by Gencorp — P33 million over 19 contracts. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña told the impeachment court that there are 15 Gencorp-Davao City deals worth P34 million in its database.

The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution. The 1987 charter explicitly prohibits the Vice President from having business interests while in office.
The Jollibee connection did not escape the prosecution and her critics, which used its slogan to take a swipe at the Vice President.
“Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensiya (the star is the flavor, the star is the evidence),” prosecutor Terry Ridon said.

blocks.caption: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses

blocks.text: “Inday, pa-Jollibee ka naman diyan (Inday, how about treating us to Jollibee),” former presidential adviser Ronald Llamas said in jest on Facebook.
Spectators of the trial might just be craving two things after Tuesday’s proceedings: a one-piece Chickenjoy, and an explanation from the Vice President. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why the CDC is excluding measles deaths in Pennsylvania even as outbreak appears to be ‘accelerating’
articles.summary:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention refuses to count four measles deaths in the state though doctors are ‘seeing new forms’ of disease

The US Centers of Disease Control and Prevention…

blocks.text: The US Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its measles dashboard on Friday – but it’s still not counting four measles deaths in Pennsylvania, where the outbreak appears to be accelerating and cases are appearing in ways providers have never seen before.

Members of Congress on Monday requested an “immediate briefing” on the decision to change how measles deaths are reported as cases continue to rise throughout the United States, reaching levels not seen in decades. A possible measles exposure was reported in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia last week.

The delay in death reporting is “curious” even after the CDC switched how it counts deaths, said Debra Houry, former CDC chief medical officer. It takes one to two days for the CDC to receive updated data to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) after states finish death investigations.
“Pennsylvania concluded the investigation on the first two deaths, so CDC would have these records by now,” Houry said.

Meanwhile, the outbreak “seems to be accelerating”, said Dr John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “And we’re seeing, actually, types of measles we’ve never seen before,” he added.

Doctors are now treating congenital measles – newborns who contracted the virus in utero or at birth – which was once exceedingly rare because most pregnant people were protected by vaccines or, before immunization, surviving measles in childhood.
“Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Goldman said. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.”

Pennsylvania has reported 731 cases, but that number is likely an undercount, he said. Frequently when patients come to the hospital with measles, they mention that others at home are sick as well – but they haven’t been tested, Goldman said. On average, one to three people for every 1,000 cases will die of measles, and one in five will be hospitalized.

The current deaths and hospital admissions in Pennsylvania are “definitely not proportional to what would be expected”, Houry said, and she believes the official numbers are “very much an undercount”. Under-testing can make it challenging to do contact tracing and sick people may not realize they need to isolate – both of which can make the spread of measles more likely.

Providers are preparing for more cases and more deaths. “It’s not rocket science. If we see more measles, we’ll see more deaths,” Goldman said. “I suspect that we’re not going to see a break until most people in most communities are immune either by vaccine or infection.”
Typically, the CDC collects data from states, including causes of death. Death certificates are issued at the state or local level; there are no federal death certificates.

But now, the agency is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to define deaths from measles. While the CDC has its own measles case definition, it has relied upon the World Health Organization’s definition of measles deaths.

Until a measles death definition is created, the CDC is relying on NCHS data, which “identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about why the death count was still delayed, or whether all deaths would receive a CDC definition.

Before this outbreak, measles deaths were rare in America; there were none for a decade. “When there aren’t deaths, you don’t need a precise definition,” Houry said. Pennsylvania developed a definition, and the CDC could consider adopting it, she said.

Erica Schwartz, the CDC director, denied in an interview that deaths were being miscounted for political reasons, pointing instead to the process of creating a definition. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have Covid, often that was called a Covid-related death,” Schwartz said, referencing misinformation about how Covid deaths were counted. In reality, Covid deaths were likely under-counted.

Pennsylvania’s definition of “measles death” clearly excludes unrelated deaths, so the bus scenario would not apply, Houry said. “Dr Schwartz’s comments are not only not helpful, but contribute to misinformation.”

But this isn’t the most important issue right now, she added. “I would focus less on the definition itself and responding to the measles outbreak, and that’s what the focus of the CDC director should be.”
Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, has cast doubt on the Pennsylvania deaths and reportedly instructed Schwartz not to include them in the CDC tally.

Kennedy only mentioned the measles outbreak once in a speech spanning nearly an hour and a half at an anti-vaccine conference on Thursday. He noted only that deaths from measles are headline news and he asked that severe side effects and deaths from vaccines get the same attention. About one to two people in a million experience severe side effects from vaccines, while with measles one in five people are hospitalized and one to three in 1,000 die.
Pennsylvania has responded aggressively to the outbreak, standing up more than 100 pop-up clinics and requesting additional vaccination support from the CDC.

The state department of health has “done a spectacular job of dealing with this”, Goldman said. Tests have a 24-hour turnaround time. “I have called them up on a Thursday before the holiday weekend and arranged for them to do testing before it closed at noon the following day,” Goldman said. “They have provided us with information, and they have provided us with really really good support.”
While there is a likely undercount of cases, “it’s not because they couldn’t get a test”, he said. “It’s because they were sick at home and did not seek medical care.”
The response hasn’t been limited to the health department, Houry noted. “Health systems and clinicians are really stepping up across the state to get vaccines to their communities.”

Before this outbreak, Goldman was the rare American doctor who had seen measles, once in 1988 and once in 1992. Between 1992 and 2026, he didn’t see a single case. Now, “we’re seeing at least one every day”, he said. He’s preparing for three to six more months of this. “Never in my life did I think I was ever going to see measles again,” he said.

He fears for other vaccine-preventable diseases: whooping cough, diphtheria, polio. “In a way, I think this is a warning,” he said. “What worries me is measles is conceivably the canary in the coal mine.”

articles.title: ‘The choice was prison or exile’: journalists who fled Russia publish grim portrait of Putin
articles.summary:
Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin, who were forced to move abroad in 2021, tell of president capable of ‘limitless cruelty’

At 6am on 29 June 2021, the Russian journalist Roman Badanin was…

blocks.text: At 6am on 29 June 2021, the Russian journalist Roman Badanin was woken by a knock on the door of his family’s Moscow apartment. “Come quickly, someone has scratched your car in the courtyard,” a voice shouted from outside. As he opened the door, masked men pushed their way in.

Across the city, a similar raid was happening at the home of Badanin’s colleague Mikhail Rubin. The masked men were officers of the FSB, the Russian intelligence service, instruments of the “climate of fear and violence” that the journalists say Vladimir Putin has imposed on Russia in their forensically detailed biography of the Russian president.

The Tsar in Person is almost 800 pages and has won the Grand Prix Strasbourg, a French literary award, whose jury said it read like a “spy novel” and praised the “courage and commitment” of the authors during decades of investigating reporting.

For Badanin and Rubin, the dawn raids were a warning. As founders of the independent media project Proekt, specialising in investigative journalism, both men had been threatened, interrogated, labelled traitors and foreign agents, banned from news events and had offices searched. Other colleagues had not been so lucky: several had died suddenly or in unexplained accidents or seemingly random attacks.

Rubin told the Guardian: “The first time we were threatened was in 2019 when we published an investigation into the chief of Putin’s propaganda operation. A Kremlin official warned me the consequences might be scary. Security agents visited my parents and asked them why I, their son, was selling out his country, betraying Russia.”

After the FSB agents’ dawn raid, Rubin discovered his passport placed carefully on a table. “It was a message. If they’d taken it, I wouldn’t be allowed to leave the country, but they wanted me to leave so they put it where I would see it,” he said. “At the time I didn’t plan on leaving. I didn’t want to overthink the danger because I thought they were just trying to stop me working.”
Less than three weeks later, the Kremlin declared Proekt an “undesirable” media outlet. “I left Moscow the next morning,” Rubin said.
Badanin, who was on holiday with his family in Morocco, decided it was too dangerous for him to return. “The choice was prison or exile and I didn’t want to go to prison.”

blocks.caption: Roman Badanin (left) and Mikhail Rubin. Composite: Wikipedia and Proekt

blocks.text: Their book, so far published only in Russian and French, charts the rise of Putin from an unremarkable clerk and undercover KGB agent at St Petersburg city hall to the Kremlin, where he has clung to power since 2000.

It is not the first biography to portray the president and his circle of cronies as cruel and corrupt, but the devil is in the encyclopaedic detail. Badanin and Rubin, both former Kremlin-accredited “pool” journalists, have 40 years of investigative journalism between them and have conducted hundreds of interviews to produce a grim portrait of Putin.

They depict him as a modern-day tsar, without ideology or convictions, a dictator capable of “limitless cruelty” who sees himself as above morality and laws. Rivals and opponent, or simply those who have become inconvenient, meet unexpected ends in accidents, crashes and falls, or are poisoned with toxins and radioactive particles causing agonising deaths.

“These pages are the result of war and repression, of exile and the death of some of those close to us, the suffering of friends thrown in prison,” the pair write. “We hope it will contribute to destroying the circumstances that have made all this misfortune possible and defeat the person who did this with his own hands.”

It is also the story of Russia from the end of the Soviet Union to today. Badanin says the book is aimed at young Russians who have no idea what their country was like before Putin took power. Unsurprisingly, it is banned by the Kremlin.

Badanin told Le Monde: “We’re also targeting audiences abroad, where many myths about Putin are circulating. There’s no need to invent myths about Putin. Let the facts reveal the truth about him and his system.
“The Kremlin leader has no ideology. The war in Ukraine has made this clear: this war is not an extension of his ideas, it is merely a means of staying in power.”

Today, even thousands of miles from Moscow, neither journalist feels entirely safe from what they call “Putin’s death squads” dispatched to murder dissident Russians abroad to demonstrate the Kremlin’s long arms.
Last year, FBI agents turned up at Badanin’s California home to warn him they had information that he was at risk of an attack “by foreign special services”.
“I feel a little bit safer here than in Europe, but not completely safe,” Badanin said.

blocks.text: US TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban
Ariana Baio
The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds.
The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights.

The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”.
“Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.”

It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950.

On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background.

The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday.
Trump set for UN meetings with war on agenda as speech looms
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump is expected to ⁠start the day with a speech to assembled delegates at the UN General Assembly, before meeting with no fewer than 11 world leaders, bilaterally or in group settings.

While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address, telling the audience that their countries were “going to hell” for, among other things, climate policy and mass migration.
The president is then set for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with ⁠leaders from four continents on Tuesday.
It comes against the backdrop of an unstable Middle East and a four-and-a-half-year-old war in Ukraine that shows no signs of abating.

Trump will meet with British prime minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian ‌president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy ‌Rodriguez, Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and the representatives of the Gulf states of the United Arab Emirates, ‌Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar.

In the evening, he may meet dozens more leaders, albeit briefly, during a leaders’ reception. Trump met with French president Emmanuel Macron on Monday and additions to his Tuesday schedule are possible.
Here, my colleague Robert Tait provides some analysis on what may be expected from Trump’s address:
In other developments:

items: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here.

The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here.

Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here.

The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here.

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here.

articles.title: Palace tells investors not to abuse gov’t trust amid ‘ghost internet’ probe
articles.summary: In her appeal to the investors, Palace spokesperson Claire Castro noted that complete payments have been made, so services must be delivered properly.

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 6:30pm
Palace Press Office Claire Castro addressed the media in a press briefing on September 22, 2026.
Screenshot from RTVM
MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang appealed to investors on Tuesday, September 22 not to abuse the government’s trust in them in providing services and products that are intended for public use.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro made the appeal in a press briefing amid the ongoing investigation of the Office of the Ombudsman on the ‘ghost internet’ scheme, or the alleged irregularities on the government’s connectivity programs.

“So panawagan naman natin sa mga ating mga kababayan at sa mga investors na ito. Kayo po ay pinagtitiwalaan ang ating pamahalaan. Huwag niyo naman pong abusuhin ang tiwalang ibinigay sa inyo,” Castro said.
(So, our appeal to our fellow countrymen and to these investors. You are trusted by our government. Please do not abuse the trust that has been given to you.)

Last week, the Ombudsman said that they had discovered an alleged scheme in the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) in which the government paid billions of public funds for outdated, overpriced, or undelivered software.
Authorities said the investigation will cover the Free Wi-fi program in which contractors allegedly installed the software without providing internet access.
According to Castro, Malacañang supports the ongoing probe by the Ombudsman, noting that the alleged irregularities will definitely affect government services and transactions.

“Kung kulang ang mga maibibigay sa ating serbisyo, hindi magiging maganda ang epekto nito. Hindi magiging effective din yung sinasabi natin na dapat lahat konektado kasi kulang-kulang ang bibigay na serbisyo,” Castro said.
(If the services we are provided are inadequate, their effects will not be good. Our goal of ensuring that everyone is connected will not be effective either because services are not enough.)
In her appeal to the investors, Castro also noted that complete payments have been made, so services must be delivered properly.
“Ang mga ibinabayad sa inyo ay kumpleto naman. So huwag niyo naman pong kulangan ang dapat na ibigay sa ating mga kababayan,” Castro said.
(You were given complete payments. So, don’t deprive our fellow countrymen of what they are entitled to.)

articles.title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
articles.summary: The UK Foreign Office says it is supporting the man's family and working with local authorities.

blocks.text: Italian authorities are searching for a British man who has gone missing after reportedly diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager.

The man was attempting to rescue two people - a father and son - who were in distress in the water near the San Siro municipality on the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, Italian media report.
The man and the family he was friends with had reportedly been on a boating trip at the time. The father and son were later rescued by another passing boat, but the man has not been seen again.
The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities."
Emergency services - including a helicopter, divers and boat units - have responded at the scene, where the lake's depth can reach more than 200m, according to Italian news agency Ansa.
Rescuers are now preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, local news site Qui Como reports.
The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (11:30 GMT) by the mother of the teenager, who was on a rented boat around 600m from shore with her other child, it said.

The man - who dived in after the father and son after they experienced difficulty swimming and was described as being in his late 30s - began to sink and was not seen resurfacing, the local newspaper reports.
The mother then called emergency services. The father and son were given medical treatment after suffering from the early stages of hypothermia, according to Qui Como.
Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows.
However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Uswag Ilonggo Rep. Ang for 90 days
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Sixth Division has ordered the preventive suspension of Rep. James Ang Dit Ang Jr. (Uswag Ilonggo Partylist) pending the resolution of the graft charges against him.

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 6:27pm
Uswag Ilonggo party-list Rep. James “Jojo” Ang
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Sixth Division has ordered the preventive suspension of Rep. James Ang Dit Ang Jr. (Uswag Ilonggo Partylist) pending the resolution of the graft charges against him.

In a resolution promulgated on September 21, the anti-graft court directed that Ang be suspended from his post as a member of the House of Representatives, as well as from any other public office he may currently or hereafter hold, for 90 days.
The suspension stems from two criminal cases charging Ang with violations of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, otherwise known as the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
The charges are premised on Ang's alleged financial or pecuniary interest in Allencon Development Corporation (Allencon), according to the anti-graft court.

In ordering the suspension, the court cited Section 13 of Republic Act No. 3019, which mandates the suspension of any incumbent public officer facing a valid criminal prosecution under the anti-graft law.
The court pointed to jurisprudence explaining that preventive suspension is mandatory once the validity of the information is established.

"The court trying a case has neither discretion nor duty to determine whether preventive suspension is required to prevent the accused from using his [or her] office to intimidate witnesses or frustrate his [or her] prosecution or continue committing malfeasance in office," the court noted, citing the Supreme Court ruling in Bolastig v. Sandiganbayan.
The Office of the Ombudsman filed 14 counts of graft against Ang Jr. on July 25.

The Ombudsman alleges that while serving in Congress, Ang held a pecuniary interest in Allencon, a construction firm that won P214 million in Department of Public Works and Highways contracts and was paid nearly P199 million.

items: Jean Claude Saclag won a silver medal in the men's traditional -65kg class at the 2026 Asian Games, marking the Philippines' best finish so far.
Saclag initially knocked down his opponent, Otabek Rajabov, but ultimately lost by unanimous decision after Rajabov utilized his ground game effectively.
The Philippines has now secured one silver and three bronze medals in the games, with notable performances from other athletes including a women's kata team in karate.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Mixed martial arts standout Jean Claude Saclag missed out on a coveted gold medal but delivered the Philippines’ best finish so far in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Saclag settled for silver, falling prey to Tajikistan’s Otabek Rajabov via unanimous decision in the final of the men’s traditional -65kg class at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Center on Tuesday, September 22.

A pride of Kalinga and Benguet, Saclag scored an early knockdown as he dropped Rajabov with a left hook to the head before the Tajik regained his bearings and banked on his prolific ground game en route to the victory.
Rajabov, an unbeaten professional MMA fighter with a 6-0 record, pulled off multiple takedowns the rest of the way to neutralize Saclag.

“It was really unfortunate. We really prepared for the ground game. I gave it my all. At least we got the silver and we’re not going home without a medal,” Saclag said in a mix of Filipino and English during the post-match Cignal broadcast.
An accomplished fighter in multiple combat disciplines, Saclag matched his silver in the 2014 edition in Incheon, South Korea, where he represented the country in wushu.
The medal is an early birthday gift for Saclag, who is also a three-time kickboxing champion in the Southeast Asian Games. He turns 32 on Friday, September 25.
Saclag reached the championship match after beating Saudi Arabia’s Saud Fawaz Almolhem in the quarterfinals and Japan’s Daisuke Murayama in the semifinals.

Earlier in the day, the karate trio of Rebecca Cyril Torres, Ysabielle Arrogante, and Samantha Emmanuelle Veguillas bagged another bronze for the country, earning a podium finish in the women’s kata team event.
The Filipinas absorbed a 5-0 loss to Iran in the semifinals but redeemed themselves with a 4-1 victory over Thailand in the bronze-medal match at the Toyohashi Gymnasium.
“It has been a long journey. My teammates have gone through a lot of hardships,” said Torres in Filipino.
“We have suffered a lot of losses over the years, but we just perform and fight until the end.”

The Philippines now has one silver and three bronzes, the other two medals coming from the women’s soft tennis team of Bien Zoleta, Princess Catindig, Hilary Paas, Shyryn Salazar, and Christy Sañosa, and mixed martial artist Carlos Alvarez. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Vermont man found guilty of attempted murder in 2023 shooting of 3 Palestinian students
articles.summary: A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defence rooted in his claims…

image.caption: Hisham Awartani testifies in court during Jason Eaton's attempted murder trial in Chittenden County Superior Court in Burlington, Vt., on Monday. Awartani, one of three men shot in the November 2023 incident, was paralyzed from the waist down as a result of his injuries. (Glenn Russell/VTDigger/The

blocks.text: World

A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defence rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies.
Defence lawyers failed to convince a jury that Jason Eaton, 51, was not sane at time of shooting
Jason Eaton faces up to life in prison in the November 2023 attack in Burlington, which paralyzed Hisham Awartani from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.

The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a weeklong trial that saw testimony from the three men, who recounted how their stroll ended in bloodshed, and defence and prosecution psychiatric experts who offered differing views of Eaton's mental health and criminal culpability.

Eaton, 51, did not testify in his own defence. He stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read, standing alongside his lawyers — public defenders whom he tried to fire last week over his concerns that his defence hadn't been "adequately presented."
Judge John Pacht, who blocked Eaton's midtrial bid to act as his own lawyer, ordered him jailed pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled.
Awartani and Aliahmad watched from the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiling and hugging people around them.

"The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry, but it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did," Awartani's mother, Elizabeth Price, told reporters afterward.
Shooter had recently lost job

The men, all 20 at the time, had been visiting Awartani's grandmother for Thanksgiving. They were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic as they walked near the University of Vermont campus after dusk. Two of them were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs.

Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. He claimed that the CIA and Mossad transmitted their orders via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbours. His lawyers had urged jurors to find him not guilty by reason of insanity, an outcome that would've spared him from prison but could have required that he undergo mental health treatment.

Eaton's lawyers, Margaret Jansch and Joshua O'Hara, said he had struggled with mental health issues his whole life, including diagnoses of attention deficit, post-traumatic stress, bipolar, depression and borderline personality disorders, culminating in a psychotic break after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting.

O'Hara told jurors that Eaton claimed he started receiving messages while listening to a local NPR affiliate. At first, the messages were encouraging and validating, the lawyer said, but subsequent messages turned dark, insisting that Eaton "has to go out and shoot somebody."

Prosecutor Sarah George countered that Eaton was a narcissist but not legally insane. He had a grandiose sense of self-importance and lacked empathy but was fully aware of the criminality of his conduct, George said in a closing argument. He repeatedly asked for a lawyer when approached by police and didn't claim at the time to be hearing messages directing his actions, she said.

Eaton didn't disclose to officers his possession of a Ruger .380-calibre handgun, later found in a bedroom dresser. Crime lab testing concluded it was used in the shooting, said George, the Chittenden County state's attorney.
Hate crime charges not filed

The shooting, weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, shook Burlington and reverberated in the West Bank, where the three wounded men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the U.S. for college. It spawned calls for a hate crime investigation.

Days after the shooting, George said in her closing argument, Eaton had told his lawyers that he wished Awartani's grandmother had warned him that the men were "going to dress up like terrorists" and trek through his neighbourhood.
But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire.

Awartani testified last week that he first noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived. Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking toward them. His face was expressionless and he didn't say anything. As Eaton got to about five to 10 feet away, "he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us," Awartani said.

Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College near Philadelphia, said he fled and hid behind another home after seeing Aliahmad fall to the ground. He said he only realized later, when he sat down, that he had also been wounded in the right buttock.
Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Rhode Island at the time, was shot in the chest and the bullet ricocheted off his scapula, causing paraplegia in his spinal cord.
Aliahmad, who was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut, was struck in the collarbone.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes as Zelenskyy attends UNGA
articles.summary: The Russian army targeted economic infrastructure in Ukraine, while Ukraine struck an oil refinery. This comes ahead of the UN General Assembly, where President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is due to meet…

image.caption: Dnipropetrovsk regional governor has said that a warehouse was damaged in the overnight strikesImage: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine traded strikes targeting infrastructure overnight, ahead of a United Nations General Assembly where the war in Ukraine is due to be widely discussed.
Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight into Tuesday killed four people, Ukrainian officials said, while also cutting the electricity supply to thousands.

The strikes took place in the cities Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram. The barrage included anti-ship and ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 212 drones.
DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation
The region of Dnipropetrovsk is the country's industrial heartland, where major production industries are located, including steel-making and machine building.
In the city of Dnipro, four people were killed and six were injured. According to Hanzha, the strike also damaged a local business and a warehouse.
Ukraine strikes Russian oil refinery; 1 killed
In Russia, Ukrainian drones killed one person and injured four in the Samara region, local authorities said. The region is home to important facilities, including oil refineries.
Moscow's Defense Ministry said it had intercepted 297 drones over various regions in Russia overnight.
Samara is located some 1,000 kilometers southeast of Russian capital Moscow.
Zelenskyy attends UN General Assembly
Russia and Ukraine have both stepped up attacks recently, as the war has dragged on for four and a half years with no end in sight.
Both parties deny targeting civilians, while also blaming each other for civilian casualties.

The latest attacks come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is planning to meet US counterpart Donald Trump in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not expected at the UN General Assembly.

The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the…

blocks.text: The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people has been highlighted by new research that finds the tropics will be among the last places to feel the benefits if the global community cuts greenhouse gas emissions to net zero.
Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to historic levels than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America.

A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan.
The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless.

The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product.

“If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. The regions that have not caused the warming are those that experience the most warming.”
King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero.

“Even when we get to net zero, we have still emitted an enormous amount of carbon into the atmosphere and its effects will continue for centuries. We can’t easily undo all that damage,” he said. “Getting to net zero sooner means we are less likely to have that long-term warming after net zero. We need to get to net zero sooner to limit that inequality.”

King said tropical ecosystems, such as some coral reefs, had mostly evolved to exist in a narrower temperature range than ecosystems at higher latitudes and would continue to be heavily affected for longer as the world cut emissions.

A separate report on the impact of climate change on the stateless, commissioned by the UN refugee agency and released with the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness, called on nations to support “the continuity of statehood” for countries facing extreme climate damage. It said those at risk included Pacific islands that were losing land to rising seas.
The agency estimated about 4.5 million people were stateless but said it accepted the number was probably much larger as stateless people were “invisible to official statistics”.
after newsletter promotion
The report said the climate crisis risked creating more stateless people through displacement after climate-driven disasters such as fire, flood and sea level rise.
University of Melbourne Associate Prof Radha Govil, a report co-author, said there was a correlation between the regions most affected by climate change and statelessness.

The report recommended countries should be helped to digitise citizenship records, and steps should be taken to ensure children were afforded citizenship if they were left without parents after a disaster.
It said the risks to children were increased if mothers were not given the same rights as fathers to confer their own nationality to their children.
“The recommendations we have set out are absolutely doable,” said Govil. “They can stave of this risk of statelessness and get ahead of this problem.”

articles.title: Male infertility is 'grossly underreported'
articles.summary: It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm.…

image.caption: It just takes one out 16 million sperm, but many men can't even manage that Image: ktsdesign/Panthermedia/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sperm counts have fallen globally by more than 51% since 1973, and the decline is accelerating. That's according to a 2026 review of studies published in the journal Antioxidants. But men are less likely to get tested than women for infertility.
"Male infertility is understated. It is so huge a problem," said Edidiong Akang, a reproductive biologist at the University of Lagos, Nigeria.

In a study led by Akang and published in the journal Scientific Reports in 2023, he and his colleagues analyzed semen samples from more than 17,000 men and found that the quality of sperm shape and size (known as sperm morphology) had deteriorated by about 50% between 2010 and 2019.
Sperm motility (how well it swims to the female egg) had also dropped significantly — in Nigeria, for example, by 87% in that same period.
And yet, as Akang told DW, the male share of infertility is "grossly underreported" and, as a result, misunderstood.
What affects a man's fertility?

Male fertility depends on a healthy sperm shape, size, motility, and its concentration and count. The latter is often used as an indication of male fertility because many millions try to reach the egg but only one or few make it. They need to be strong swimmers.
Why do some healthy embryos fail to implant in the uterus?
These factors depend on other, underlying health conditions: Male infertility can be caused by weight gain, stress, poor sleep, smoking, microplastics and cannabis use.
Weight gain in particular effects the testes (also: testicles), which produce sperm and hormones like testosterone.
The testes function best at two degrees centigrade cooler than the rest of the body. Fat raises the temperature, and that can affect the sperm — its concentration, count and motility.
Why male infertility often goes undiagnosed

Male sexual health is often overlooked, possibly because men under the age of 40 don't generally have a regular reason to get checked — if you're older than 40, you may get your prostate checked annually. But even a urologist won't check your sperm count unless you ask them.
Women, on the other hand, get a monthly signal — their menstrual cycle — and may be able to infer from that that something is wrong.
A man gets no such natural signals about his fertility until he tries to conceive with a woman. And by then he may be 30 or 40, when some health outcomes are hard to reverse.
Riffat Bibi, a clinical embryologist who has led an IVF laboratory in Pakistan for 17 years, described what men often say on arrival: "Okay, check my wife first."
Sometimes a mother-in-law brings the daughter-in-law, which also suggests that the mother-in-law thinks: It can't be my son's fault.
And some patients "feel sexual activity is equivalent to fertility, which it is not," said Bibi.
Roughly 80% of Bibi's cases now involve a male factor, far above the 50-50 split long assumed, and her laboratory has had to adapt, she said.

They are also seeing this development in IVF (in vitro fertilization) treatment. Sperm has become so poor that nearly all her clients need an embryologist to pick a single sperm and inject it directly into the egg.
But there is another factor than many men don't talk about much: synthetic testosterone — or steroids.
IVF explained: Process, costs & risks
Testosterone shuts down sperm production
Some men, keen on a muscley body, suppress their own sperm production unknowingly by taking anabolic steroids, a synthetic form of testosterone.

The appeal of anabolic steroids is straightforward, said Harrison Pope, a Harvard Medical School researcher: Steroids enhance athletic performance. A steroid user, who drinks, smokes and skips half of his workouts can outperform a dedicated, clean athlete.
Pope, who has studied steroids for three decades, said "they are highly effective."
But what you gain in athletic performance, you lose in fertility, because an over-supply of testosterone can shut down sperm production.
A healthy body will keep testosterone levels in balance. Too little testosterone can also impede sperm production.
Sperm production can restart if you stop taking testosterone supplements, but Pope said it depends on your age, and much you were taking and for how long.
Occasional steroid users usually regain a "normal" sperm count. The World Health Organization considers a normal sperm count to be about 16 million sperm per milliliter of semen (or higher).
Heavy, long-term steroid users, meanwhile, often do not recover or return to normal sperm production.

Users typically take steroids in cycles – weeks on the drug, followed by a a break to let the body recover. But when Dutch researchers followed 100 men through one cycle of steroids and for a year after, they found two-thirds still had very low sperm counts, some had no sperm at all, and a year later, their counts had still not returned to normal.

Not everyone takes steroids, and yet falling sperm counts still occur. Take India, for example, where Chirag Bhandari, runs the Institute of Andrology and Sexual Health in Jaipur. Bhandari estimates that steroids account for less than 0.1% of the country's falling sperm counts. Overweight, heat-stress and smoking are usually the cause.

If a man is tested early, his sperm count will often return to normal within six to twelve months, both Bhandari and Bibi said. But the longer the problem goes undetected, the less likely that becomes.

articles.title: PH, EU on ‘clear path’ to free trade agreement. How close is a deal, really?
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declares that the EU and the Philippines have 'just agreed' on a free trade deal that could eventually make nearly all bilateral goods trade…

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declares that the EU and the Philippines have 'just agreed' on a free trade deal that could eventually make nearly all bilateral goods trade tariff-free, with signing targeted for 2027
MANILA, Philippines – A “substantial agreement,” a “clear path” toward conclusion, and from the European Commission president herself: “We just agreed on a EU-Philippines free trade deal!”

After years of negotiations, officials from the Philippines and European Union (EU) spoke on Tuesday, September 22, with resounding confidence that a long-awaited free trade agreement (FTA) between the two was within reach.
But beneath the diplomatic jargon, is there actually an FTA already? Not quite.

Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maroš Šefčovič announced that both sides had reached a “substantial agreement” following a video call, with their joint statement describing the development as a “breakthrough” that puts the FTA on a “clear path towards its formal conclusion in the coming months.”
Negotiating teams were instructed to finalize the agreement “as soon as possible.”

Meanwhile, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen struck a more emphatic tone in a post on X after speaking with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., declaring that the two sides had “just agreed” on a free trade deal. The Commission’s official readout of their September 21 call was more cautious, saying the Philippines and EU were “about to conclude talks” on an FTA.

So what’s left to do? A separate European Commission press release states that the Philippines and EU still have to “now finalize the negotiations on the basis of the substantial agreement reached today, including determining its implementation and finalizing technical details.”
There is already a target for the next big milestone. European Commission President von der Leyen said she looks forward to returning to the Philippines in 2027 to sign the FTA.

The European Commission said the deal would remove or cut tariffs on more than 94% of product categories, covering over 97% of the goods the Philippines and EU currently trade by value. It also covers services and investment, digital trade, intellectual property, food and product standards, sustainability, energy, and raw materials.

It would also establish rules allowing foreign bidders access to the Philippine government procurement market, which the EU described as opening that market to foreign bidders “for the first time ever.”
For Filipinos, the most immediate question is whether an FTA could make European products cheaper.

Potentially, yes. The EU says some of its major industrial exports to the Philippines include machinery and appliances, transport equipment, medicines and medical appliances, while agricultural exports include pork, poultry, dairy products and spirits.

Cutting Philippine tariffs on these goods could reduce their landed cost and increase competition or consumer choice. But an FTA doesn’t automatically mean cheaper shelf prices. It is still unclear which individual products will get immediate tariff elimination and which may be phased in over several years.
The EU was the Philippines’ fourth-largest trading partner in 2025, accounting for 8.3% of total Philippine goods trade.

Bilateral merchandise trade reached €17.6 billion (P1.27 trillion)* in 2025, consisting of €9.5 billion (P684.3 billion) in EU imports from the Philippines and €8.1 billion (P583.4 billion) in EU exports to the country. Services trade reached another €10.3 billion (P741.9 billion) in 2024, while the stock of EU foreign direct investment in the Philippines stood at €15.4 billion (P1.11 trillion).

The negotiations themselves have been more than a decade in the making. Talks were launched in 2015, stalled after a second negotiating round in 2017, and revived in March 2024 after both sides conducted a technical stocktaking exercise. – Rappler.com
*€1 = P72.0305 based on the September 22, 2026 rate of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ Daily Reference Exchange Rate Bulletin

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Bill postponing 2026 barangay, SK polls not yet a law as of September 22
articles.summary: In a September 18 statement, the Commission on Elections said the November 2026 barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections will proceed as there is yet no law for its postponement

blocks.text: Claim: The bill postponing the November 2 barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) became a law on September 21, prompting the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to announce the suspension of the filing of certificates of candidacy.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook account named “Rolando Hagos,” which currently has over 20,000 followers, has made multiple posts bearing the false claim.
His most recent post says: “Comelec, kinansel na ang filing of candidacy ng mga tatakbo para sa barangay election.”
(The Comelec has cancelled the filing of certificates of candidacy for those running in the barangay elections.)
He also made other posts earlier claiming, “September 21 ganap ng batas ang postponement ng BSKE. November 2028 na.”
(The postponement of the BSKE became law on September 21. It is now set for November 2028.)
Both posts have received a total of 2,000 reactions, more than 600 comments, and less than 100 shares, as of writing.
The facts: In a September 18 statement posted on Facebook, Comelec Chairman George Erwin said the BSKE will push through on November 2, unless a new law postponing the election will be enacted.

In his statement, the chair explained: “Tuloy na tuloy ang (BSKE) eleksyon hanggang sa araw na ‘to, sapagkat ‘yun po ang batas. ‘Yan po ang ikalat n’yo. ‘Yan po ay hindi fake news; totoo po ‘yan. Wala pa tayong batas. Batas ang ating hahanapin.”

(The election will definitely push through as scheduled, because that is what the law says. Please spread the word. That is not fake news; it is the truth. We do not have a new law yet; the law is what we look for.)

The chair also noted that unless such a law is passed, the filing of certificates of candidacy scheduled from September 28 to October 5 will push through. The commission also said that it will continue its preparation for the BSKE, in line with the provisions of Republic Act No. 12232 setting the date of elections on November 2.

The misleading posts about the postponement of the BSKE circulated after the Senate approved on September 14 a bill fixing the term of barangay and SK officials to five years, effectively moving the polls to the second Monday of November starting in 2028.

The proposed measure is now in the hands of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who may sign the bill into law or veto it. It may also lapse into law if he does not act on the measure within 30 days of receiving it.

No official government announcement or credible media report shows that the bill has already been signed into law. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro also said Marcos will review the provisions of the bill before making a decision.

BSKE postponement: This is not the first time proposals have been made to postpone the BSKE. In 2022, the elections originally scheduled for December were moved to October 2023, under Republic Act No. 11935. Following this, Republic Act No. 12232 was signed into law in August 2025 pushing the December 2025 BSKE to November 2026.
The current proposal, which aims to move the scheduled November 2026 elections to 2028, has drawn opposition from election watchdog groups.
Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked other false claims related to earlier and upcoming elections:

items: FACT CHECK: Comelec debunks claim of ACMs altering votes in Lanao del Sur
FACT CHECK: Photos of Sara Duterte visiting MILF camp ahead of 2026 polls are fake
FACT CHECK: News of 39 soldiers held by MILF is from 2023, not recent

blocks.text: – Jerome Santos/Rappler.com
John Jerome Santos is a research and data volunteer writer at Rappler. He is a fourth year Bachelor of Science in Accountancy student at the Dr. Gloria Lacson Foundation Colleges of Cabanatuan City.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
articles.summary: An initiative to show that LFW is "bigger than London" launched this year - but will it make a difference?

blocks.text: The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.
Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world?
The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London".
Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said.
A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022.
However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds.

"A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy.
"But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat.

"I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls.

"Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper."
Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be?
Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle.
She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House.
"London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old.
"You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do."
Bennett says you can harness the power of being different.
"Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says.
Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving.
"The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old.
This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital.
"I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says.
"There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland".
Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week.
The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry.
"Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion.
"There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says.
For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world.
"Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

items: The Department of Education is under pressure to accelerate the hiring process for over 20,000 unfilled teaching positions.
The 2027 National Expenditure Program proposes a budget of P976 billion for the DepEd, including P31 billion for hiring new personnel.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Education (DepEd) was told to accelerate its hiring process as it has yet to fill over 20,000 teaching positions across the country.
“Why is it taking so long to hire or to fill up these positions?” asked ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio during House plenary deliberations on Tuesday, September 22.

“Hindi maintindihan in the field bakit hindi kayo makapag-fill ng position. Maraming nag-aantay sa RQA (Registry of Qualified Applicants). Dapat matiyak na magkaroon ng mas mabilis na hiring,” Tinio also said.
(We cannot understand in the field why the DepEd cannot fill the positions. Many are waiting in the Registry of Qualified Applicants. The education department should ensure a faster hiring process.)
Tinio’s comments came as he clarified with the DepEd if there is no request for new teaching items next year.

“On teacher hiring, the department is on its continuous hiring process until this year and until next year. This is because the allocation or appropriation given to the department from the GAA (General Appropriations Act) 2026 is still being implemented,” said Davao de Oro 1st District Representative Maria Carmen Zamora.

Speaking on behalf of the DepEd as its budget sponsor, Zamora said there were 8,688 unfilled positions from the newly created items in the 2026 national budget. There were also more than 12,000 vacancies from previous years.

Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the education department may get P976 billion. Over P31 billion is earmarked for the hiring of new school personnel, which already includes the thousands of unfilled teaching positions.
The DepEd also explained that the 2027 budget proposal allocated P12 billion for the promotion of 135,000 teachers under the Expanded Career Progression System.
But the agency is still pushing for its “wishlist,” which seeks an additional P4.29 billion to hire over 14,000 more entry-level teachers.
Tinio also brought to the plenary what he said was the sentiment of public school counselors in the country.
“Medyo nade-demoralize daw sila kasi ang DepEd panay ang mga statement announcing na may malaking pondo para sa pag-hire ng school counselor associates,” the lawmaker said.
(They’re demoralized as the DepEd only talks about the big budget for hiring school counselor associates.)
“Sabi nila, ‘Eh kaming matagal dito na guidance counselor, eh mukhang malalampasan pa ng starting salary ng mga school counselor associates na kaming mamamahala sa kanila,’” he said.
(They said, “We, guidance counselors, might end up having lower starting salaries compared with school counselor associates, who will work under our supervision.”)

The DepEd is currently hiring school counselor associates, who do not need a license, to expand mental health services in public schools. They have a starting rate of Salary Grade 11, which is the same with incumbent school counselors.
The Philippines has a severe shortage of licensed guidance counselors, with only around 1,000 working under the education department.
According to Zamora, the DepEd already requested the reclassification of school counselors to Salary Grade 16 with the Department of Budget and Management.
The DepEd’s budget wishlist also includes boosting the compensation for asatidz, or teachers of Arabic language and Islamic values education under the Madrasah education program.
If approved, the monthly pay for asatidz may increase to P16,000 from the current P12,000 rate, according to Zamora.
The DepEd also committed to absorb Islamic Studies and Arabic Language teachers from the Bangsamoro’s Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education into the DepEd by January 2027.

While satisfied with these updates, Akbayan Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula flagged the decrease for the Madrasah education program from P521 million in the 2026 GAA to P504 million in the 2027 NEP.

“Naninindigan kami na ang pondo para sa Madrasah education program, dapat ma-restore man lang sa 2026 GAA level upang matiyak ang sapat na compensation at suporta para sa ating asatidz at Muslim learners,” Ismula said.
(We maintain that the funding for the Madrasah education program must be restored to the 2026 GAA level to ensure enough compensation and support for our asatidz and Muslim learners.) – Rappler.com

blocks.text: EU deadlocked over plans to remove two Russian billionaires from sanctions list

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels

The EU is deadlocked over a plan to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list as part of a bitterly disputed deal to keep broader restrictions in place on nearly 3,000 people and companies accused of enabling Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Russian businessman and founder of USM Holdings Alisher Usmanov during an awarding ceremony at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia in 2018. Photograph: SPUTNIK/Reuters

blocks.text: Ambassadors from the EU’s 27 member states failed to reach agreement at a meeting early on Tuesday – their third session in around 24 hours on the topic. The senior diplomats will reconvene later today just hours ahead of a legal deadline.
Without an agreement sanctions on nearly 3,000 people and entities accused of supporting the war on Ukraine will lapse at the end of Tuesday 22 September.
The list includes Vladimir Putin, foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, Duma deputies, Russia’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
The EU can also agree a short-term extension pending a longer agreement and has already prolonged the deadline by one week. One diplomat suggested that was a likely outcome.
Latvia emerged as the last-minute block on an agreement. Like many member states the Baltic state has strong objections to the de-listings, which are demanded by France and Slovakia.

Latvia’s prime minister Andris Kulbergs tweeted late Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise – the de-listings of Usmanov and Fridman in exchange for a 36-month extension of the blacklist of nearly 3,000 names, far longer than the usual six-month rollover.
He said:
“Extending sanctions for 36 months would be the right step. However, the price for it must not be simply striking both individuals from the sanctions list. Latvia cannot accept SUCH an offer.”

blocks.caption: Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs attends the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland last week. Photograph: Kaisa Siren/EPA

blocks.text: He added that his foreign minister, Baiba Braže, would work with “Brussels and Paris to find a solution SUITABLE for Latvia’s interests. We will seek support in the EUROPEAN UNION for Latvia’s position”.

When details of the expected deal emerged on Monday, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the delisting was “unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase”.

France infuriated and stunned EU member states by joining Slovakia’s populist government in petitioning for Usmanov’s de-listing earlier this month. France has told EU diplomats only that the delisting is on national security grounds. The Financial Times has reported that it is linked to a prisoner exchange deal with Azerbaijan involving the release of French nationals.

Azerbaijan, along with the Organisation of Turkic States, has previously lobbied western decision-makers to remove Usmanov from sanctions listings, describing him as “a renowned philanthropist” who has built bridges between the West, Central Asia and wider Turkic world. Slovakia began lobbying for Usmanov and fellow billionaire Mikhail Fridman to be removed from the EU sanctions list in the summer.
Luxembourg has argued that Fridman should come off the list, if Usmanov is removed. Fridman is seeking $16bn in damages from Luxembourg for freezing his assets.

blocks.text: At least 11 people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey after an attacker opened fire before fleeing the scene.
The incident happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Turkey's western province of Manisa at about 08:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
The attacker has since been detained, according to the local governor's office.
Local media reported that two of the victims taken to hospital were in critical conditions.
CCTV footage posted online appeared to show a male on a street near the school carrying a firearm, with other clips apparently showing him fleeing still carrying the weapon.
The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear.
It has been reported in Turkish media that the gunman is a 15-year-old student, though that has not been officially confirmed.
In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular".
It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa.
